title: Your marketing plan is probably a list of jobs. Start with the bottleneck instead.
markdown:
# Your marketing plan is probably a list of jobs. Start with the bottleneck instead.

At 9:17 on Monday morning, the founder had six browser tabs open: a half-finished newsletter, last week's social calendar, an ad dashboard, two competitor homepages, and a notes file titled "Q4 marketing." By noon, the list had grown. Nothing had shipped.

That scene is familiar in small teams because marketing arrives as a pile of plausible work. Post more often. Refresh the landing page. Start a webinar. Run search ads. Improve onboarding. Each task may be sensible. The hard part is deciding which one deserves this week's scarce attention.

You do not need a grand marketing strategy to make that decision. You need a working diagnosis, one move that follows from it, and a way to tell whether it helped. This article gives you a small-team planning method that produces those three things without pretending you have a department behind you.

## Stop calling every problem a traffic problem

When a team says it needs more marketing, it often means revenue feels stuck. That is an outcome, not a diagnosis. More visitors will not repair an offer people do not understand. More content will not fix a signup flow that drops interested people at the first form. More ads will only make a weak activation problem more expensive.

Start by placing the problem in one part of the path:

- People do not reach you: discovery is the constraint.
- People reach you but do not act: the message, offer, or page is the constraint.
- People sign up but do not get value: activation is the constraint.
- People get value once but do not return or buy: retention or conversion is the constraint.

These labels are deliberately plain. Their value is that they rule work out. If a trial signup rate has fallen while relevant traffic is steady, another top-of-funnel content sprint is hard to justify this week. Look at the page, the offer, and the path after the click first.

Write the evidence in one sentence. "We had roughly the same qualified visits this month, but fewer people started a trial after the pricing-page change" is usable. "Our marketing feels weak" is not. The sentence does not need perfect attribution. It needs enough shape to prevent a meeting from becoming a menu of tactics.

## Pick a move that changes the constrained step

Once you have a candidate bottleneck, choose one action that can alter it inside a short window. A useful move has an owner, an asset, a distribution point, and one metric. If it needs a new brand platform, five approvals, and a six-week production cycle, it is not the move for a team that is already stretched.

Suppose prospects read your product page but do not request a demo. The move may be to replace a feature-led opening with a short problem-led section, then send the same message in a follow-up email to people who visited that page. The asset is the new opening and email. The distribution point is the page and follow-up. The metric is demo requests from that audience.

That is a plan. "Improve positioning" is a wish wearing business language.

The same test works for content. If discovery is the constraint, do not promise to "do SEO." Choose a question your best prospects repeatedly ask before buying, make a useful page that answers it, decide where it will be distributed, and define the signal you will inspect. A single published answer with a distribution decision beats a calendar full of titles no one owns.

## Give the work a stopping rule

Small teams lose time when every campaign becomes an open-ended project. Set the review date before you make the asset. For example: publish the revised page on Tuesday, send the email on Wednesday, and review qualified demo requests the following Wednesday. Decide in advance what would make you keep, revise, or retire the move.

The result may be inconclusive. That is still useful if you recorded the audience, the promise, the asset, and the metric. You can then change one part deliberately instead of rewriting everything because the week felt disappointing.

Avoid the temptation to call every weak result a distribution failure. A message can miss because the audience was wrong, the promise was vague, the page asked for too much, or the product was not the answer to that problem. The point of a short test is not to protect the original idea. It is to make the next decision less foggy.

## Use a brief that someone can execute

Before assigning the work, fill in this brief in plain language:

> **Audience:** Who is experiencing the problem now?
>
> **Observed constraint:** What behavior or number makes you think this is the narrowest point?
>
> **One move:** What will change this week?
>
> **Asset:** What page, email, post, offer, or script must exist?
>
> **Distribution:** Where will the intended audience encounter it?
>
> **Metric and review date:** What will you inspect, and when?

If two people fill this in and produce different answers, the disagreement is productive. You have found the decision that needs discussion before the team spends another week producing content by default.

## When you need a second set of reasoning

The difficult part is usually not knowing that funnels exist. It is choosing a move when several explanations sound possible and nobody on the team has the time to play a full-time marketer.
